fields.name: Bara
fields.short_description: Bara is a Newari snack. It is commonly known as 'Wo' in Newari language. This traditional food among Newari people symbolises good luck during festivals, birthdays, weddings and other occasions.

fields.name: Samay Baji
fields.short_description: Samay Baji is a traditional Newari platter of assorted dishes, often served during festivals, celebrations, and rituals, symbolizing good luck, health, and prosperity. It typically includes beaten rice, puffed rice, fried soybeans, meat (often buffalo), lentil pancakes, and local wine (Ailaa or Chhyaang). It's a versatile dish, enjoyed as a snack, starter, or part of a larger feast.

fields.name: Chatamari
fields.short_description: Chatamari is a traditional Newari rice crepe, often called "Newari pizza," popular in Nepal. It's a thin, crispy flatbread made from rice flour, and can be topped with a variety of ingredients like minced meat (buffalo or chicken), eggs, onions, and cilantro. Vegetarian and vegan options with toppings like sugar or vegetables are also common. It's a versatile dish enjoyed as a snack or appetizer, especially during festivals.

fields.history:
Bara, also known as Wo, has roots in the ancient Newar civilization of the Kathmandu Valley.

It has been a staple food for centuries, especially among Newars during religious and festive occasions.

Originally made from black lentils, its simple preparation reflects agrarian lifestyles of early Nepal.

Variations of Bara have evolved over generations, including egg and meat fillings introduced later.

It continues to be passed down through oral tradition and home recipes, preserving its authenticity.
fields.cultural_significance:
Bara holds deep ritual importance and is commonly served during Newari festivals like Sithi Nakha and Mha Puja.

It symbolizes purity and nourishment, often prepared during family gatherings and communal celebrations.

In many Newar households, making Bara is a shared cultural act bonding generations.

It’s offered as part of Samay Baji sets and during religious feasts and life-cycle ceremonies.

Beyond rituals, Bara today represents Newar culinary pride and is celebrated in street food culture across Nepal.

fields.description:
Bara is a Newari snack. It is commonly known as 'Wo' in Newari language. This traditional food among Newari people symbolises good luck during festivals, birthdays, weddings and other occasions.

In appearance, it looks like a savoury rice-flour pancake. It is served with Newari drinks like 'Aila' and 'Chayang'. It is made from lentils paste after it is mixed with garlic ginger, turmeric and salt. It can be eaten with eggs or minced meat on the top.
fields.instructions:
Soak lentils in a large bowl of water overnight.
Grind it finely next day.
Add 1-2 tbsp of water to make smooth batter if needed.  It shouldn’t be in the liquid form or very thick.
Once the batter is ready, add salt, turmeric, garlic and ginger paste. (see carousel image 2)
Whisk it for a couple of minutes.
Heat 1/2 tbsp of oil in a non-stick pan or cast-iron pan.
Slowly pour the paste into the pan and spread it to make a circle shape with the spatula. Or, add some oil on your palm, take some paste in your palm and make it into a circle before putting it into the hot oil.  (see carousel image 3)
When one side turns a bit brown, turn over to the other side.
When both sides are brown it is ready. 
Serve hot with a drink.

fields.name: Bhaktapur Durbar Square
fields.shortdescription: Bhaktapur Durbar Square is a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Nepal, known for its stunning Newar architecture, temples, and royal palaces. It reflects the grandeur of the Malla dynasty and the rich cultural heritage of Bhaktapur.
fields.description:
Bhaktapur Durbar Square, located in the ancient city of Bhaktapur, is one of the most famous historical landmarks in Nepal.
It served as the royal palace of the Malla kings who ruled over the Kathmandu Valley.
The square is a living museum of traditional Newari architecture, art, and craftsmanship.
It houses magnificent temples like Vatsala Temple, Nyatapola Temple, and Bhairabnath Temple.
The 55-Window Palace, built in the 15th century, is a central attraction.
Golden Gate, richly decorated with mythological motifs, leads into the royal courtyard.
The square is paved with red bricks, adding to its timeless charm.
It features intricately carved wooden structures and stone statues.
Each monument holds religious, historical, or artistic importance.
The area is pedestrian-only, preserving its ancient ambiance.
It is a popular destination for both tourists and heritage scholars.
Festivals such as Biska Jatra bring the square to life every year.
Local artisans continue to maintain and restore its beauty.
Bhaktapur Durbar Square is a testament to Nepal’s medieval urban planning.
It represents a fusion of religion, culture, and architecture.
fields.history:
Bhaktapur Durbar Square’s origins trace back to the 12th century.
It flourished under the Malla dynasty, especially in the 15th to 18th centuries.
King Yaksha Malla established Bhaktapur as an independent kingdom in the 15th century.
Many structures, including the 55-Window Palace, were built during his reign.
The Malla kings were known as patrons of art, architecture, and culture.
Temples, palaces, and courtyards were constructed to reflect divine inspiration and power.
The square became a cultural and administrative center of the kingdom.
After King Bhupatindra Malla, the square saw artistic and religious enhancement.
The square remained significant even after the unification of Nepal by Prithvi Narayan Shah.
Though damaged by earthquakes (notably in 1934 and 2015), many structures survived or were restored.
UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 1979.
International support has helped in its reconstruction efforts post-2015 earthquake.
Bhaktapur remained relatively untouched by modern development, preserving its medieval charm.
Local communities have historically been involved in its upkeep.
Its history is deeply interwoven with the religious and political story of the Kathmandu Valley.
fields.cultural_significance:
Bhaktapur Durbar Square is a symbol of Nepal’s medieval art and cultural identity.
It showcases the excellence of Newar craftsmanship in wood, metal, and stone.
The square remains a center for traditional festivals and rituals.
Major events like Biska Jatra and Dashain are celebrated with grandeur here.
It reflects the fusion of Hindu and Buddhist traditions.
Many temples are still active, drawing devotees and tourists alike.
Cultural dances and performances often take place in the courtyards.
Artisans and local residents continue centuries-old craft traditions nearby.
It is a source of pride and spiritual significance for Bhaktapur locals.
The square serves as a cultural archive and an educational site for future generations.

fields.name: Nyatapola Temple
fields.shortdescription: Nyatapola Temple is a five-storied pagoda-style temple located in Taumadhi Square, Bhaktapur. It is the tallest temple in Nepal.
fields.description: Standing at 30 meters tall, the Nyatapola Temple is dedicated to Siddhi Lakshmi, a powerful Tantric goddess. The temple’s architecture is admired for its symmetry, strength, and detailed wood, stone, and metal carvings. The five-tiered roof and the wide plinth guarded by stone sculptures of mythical beings make it visually impressive.
fields.history: Built in 1702 AD during the reign of King Bhupatindra Malla, it was constructed to withstand natural disasters like earthquakes, which it has done remarkably well. Its name “Nyatapola” means “five-tiered” in the Newari language, symbolizing the five basic elements: earth, water, fire, air, and sky.
fields.cultural_significance: Nyatapola is more than a temple—it's a symbol of Bhaktapur’s religious devotion, architectural skill, and cultural pride. It plays a vital role during local festivals like Biska Jatra, where it becomes a central site of celebration. Its design reflects the Malla era’s blend of religion, art, and engineering excellence.

fields.name: 55-Window Palace (Pachpanna Jhyal Durbar)
fields.shortdescription: The 55-Window Palace is an iconic palace situated in Bhaktapur Durbar Square, known for its intricately carved wooden windows and impressive facade.
fields.description: This palace is a three-storied brick building with fifty-five beautifully carved wooden windows on its façade. It features traditional Newari architectural elements like latticed windows, ornate cornices, and spacious courtyards. It is part of a larger royal complex that includes temples and courtyards like the Taleju Temple and the Golden Gate.
fields.history: Commissioned by King Yaksha Malla in the 15th century and renovated by King Bhupatindra Malla in the 17th century, the palace served as a royal residence and administrative center during the Malla dynasty. The Golden Gate (Sun Dhoka), the entrance to the palace, is considered one of the finest examples of metalwork in Nepal.
fields.cultural_significance: The palace stands as a testament to the power and prosperity of the Malla kings. It represents the peak of medieval Nepali architecture and craftsmanship. As a UNESCO World Heritage site, it draws visitors from all over the world and remains a source of local pride and historical importance.

fields.name: Dattatreya Temple
fields.shortdescription: Dattatreya Temple is a unique triple-roofed temple located in Dattatreya Square, Bhaktapur, dedicated to the deity Dattatreya—believed to be a combined form of Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva.
fields.description: The temple has a distinctive architectural style with elaborate wood carvings and metal embellishments. The two guardian sculptures at the entrance and the statue of Dattatreya inside reflect the temple’s spiritual depth. Surrounding the temple are other historically significant buildings and the famous "Woodcarving Museum."
fields.history: Originally built in 1427 AD by King Yaksha Malla, legends claim the temple was constructed using timber from a single tree. It has undergone various restorations over centuries, yet retains its traditional charm. It is one of the oldest temples in Bhaktapur.
fields.cultural_significance: The temple is revered by both Hindus and Newar Buddhists. Dattatreya is viewed as a symbol of unity among the Hindu trinity. The temple is a vital location for cultural events, spiritual rituals, and traditional music performances. It also reflects Bhaktapur’s long-standing traditions in wood carving and craftsmanship.

fields.title: Sindoor Jatra
fields.description: Sindoor Jatra, also known as Biska Jatra, is a vibrant festival celebrated in Madhyapur Thimi, Nepal, on the second day of Baisakh, marking the Nepali New Year and the arrival of spring. The festival is characterized by a lively procession of 32 palanquins (khats) carrying deities through the town, with participants joyfully smearing each other with sindoor (vermillion powder) and showering it from windows and rooftops. This colorful display, accompanied by traditional music and dancing, symbolizes good fortune, unity, and the community's enduring bonds.

fields.title: Biska Jatra
fields.description: Biska Jatra, also known as Bisket Jatra, is a vibrant and ancient festival celebrated in Bhaktapur, Nepal, marking the end of the old Nepali year and the beginning of the new one. This nine-day festival is filled with chariot processions, the erection and collapse of a towering pole ("Yosing"), and the pulling of chariots carrying deities Bhairab and Bhadrakali. It's a time of cultural and religious significance, with rituals, dances, and the throwing of sindoor (vermillion powder).

fields.title: Musical Concert
fields.description: A "musical night" typically refers to an evening event focused on musical performances, either as a concert or a social gathering with music as a central element. It can involve live music performances, often with multiple artists or bands, or simply be a social setting where people enjoy music together.
